question: Many claims for damages have been filed against vaccine manufacturers. Most recently, a woman brought an action before the Frankfurt Regional Court (judgment of 14 April 2024, case No 2-12 O 264/22)1. She claims to have suffered serious side-effects following the vaccine, including constant migraines, mental impairment, heart palpitations and permanent immunodeficiencies.

She also reported that her quality of life had deteriorated significantly, pointing to difficulties concentrating, hypercoagulability and heart valve defects – all of which she attributes to the vaccine. Her claim was dismissed, however, on the grounds that she would have been previously aware of the side-effects.

What is more, the ‘binding legal effect of an administrative act’ (the vaccine authorisation in this case) is such that ‘where the relevant administrative authority has issued an effective administrative act expressly authorising a specific conduct – as with an authorisation – the admissibility of said conduct shall not be subject to judicial review by the civil courts until such time as the administrative act has been revoked or otherwise annulled by the relevant authority or an administrative court (Neue Juristische Wocheschrift 2023, 2259)’ 1.
What measures is the Commission using to support people who can prove personal injury as a result of the COVID-19 vaccine?
How is it working together with the Member States to ensure transparent communication and reporting on the side-effects brought on by the COVID-19 vaccine?

Does it still stand behind its earlier decision to grant an authorisation for COVID-19 vaccines, even though many side-effects have been reported and the vaccines have not proven to be as effective as the manufacturers promised and the public was made to expect?
answer: The indemnification clauses in the Advanced Purchase Agreements and Purchase Agreements for COVID-19 vaccines outline the obligations and responsibilities of the parties involved regarding potential losses, damages, liabilities, or legal claims arising from the contract or related activities.

However, the Commission has no comprehensive overview of cases where liability for COVID-19 vaccines has been recognised at national level as this falls under Member States’ responsibility. A transparent EU pharmacovigilance system is in place for medicines and also applies to COVID-19 authorised vaccines.

Any new information is included in the product information as soon as relevant scientific evidence is available. Where appropriate, the Commission can take regulatory actions. The Commission authorised COVID-19 vaccines based on recommendations of the European Medicines Agency (EMA) concluding a positive benefit risk balance after assessing the medicine safety, efficacy and quality.

As mentioned in reply to Question E-003117/2023 (2), an unprecedented high number of people has been administered COVID-19 vaccines (3) and the number of reported suspected side effects for these vaccines is consequently higher in total numbers. It is important to highlight that medical events occurring in vaccinated people are not necessarily caused by the COVID-19 vaccine.
EMA and national authorities evaluate data on reported events in EudraVigilanc e (4) to determine whether there is any signal indicating causality and take action as appropriate.

As referred to in reply to Question E-001200/2023 (5), most suspected side effects recorded in EudraVigilance are not eventually confirmed as causally associated and the same applies for COVID-19 vaccines.
